metadata.title: Practising In Its Sleep
metadata.note: KID-FRIENDLY explainer of a from-scratch World Models notebook (VAE + memory + controller evolved in the dream, on 16x16 Catch). This reel TEACHES. Every figure parsed from recorded outputs under 9 assertions, three of which encode the argument itself (memory roughly doubles the catch rate; the dreamer beats the sighted cheat; the loop improves on it). Build also audits dense scenes for >=12s narration, after that pacing bug recurred twice. NO INDIVIDUAL IS NAMED. Bella (af_bella).

beats.narration_text: A machine learned to play a game by practising in its sleep. It built a little copy of the world inside its own head, trained there, and then — having never once touched the real game — went and played it rather well. This is Humanitarians AI.

props.command: Walk me through a world model: squeezing what it sees into a few numbers, learning to predict what happens next, then training a player entirely inside that prediction. Show me whether the player actually works in the real game.
output: then practise somewhere that does not exist

beats.narration_text: Here is the whole game. A ball falls down a little sixteen-by-sixteen grid, and a paddle at the bottom can go left, go right, or stay put. Catch the ball. That is everything.

Before anything clever, how hard is it? Moving at random catches 28 percent of balls. A simple chaser that always slides towards the ball catches 61 percent. And something that knows exactly where the ball will land catches every single one. So 28 is hopeless, 61 is decent, and 100 is perfect.

props.headline: 28% by luck. 61% by chasing. 100% if you truly know.
props.kicker: those are the marks to beat

beats.narration_text: Now the problem at the heart of this. Look at one single picture of the game. The ball is right there, in the middle. So which way is it going? You cannot tell. It might be drifting left, it might be drifting right, and those two possibilities end in completely different places. A photograph shows you where things are. It never shows you where they are heading.

So, first job. Take each picture, all 256 little squares of it, and squash it down into just 8 numbers. That is 32x smaller. It sounds like you would lose almost everything — but when you build the picture back out of those 8 numbers, 99.3% of the time every single square comes back exactly right.

And the notebook checks something careful here. Is the ball's position really hidden in those 8 numbers, or did it get lost? Looked at in a simple straight-line way, you can barely find it. But looked at properly, by comparing against similar pictures, you can recover it perfectly. The information is all there. It is just not written in a tidy order.

props.headline: Hidden, but not lost.
props.kicker: scrambled is not the same as missing

beats.narration_text: Next, the memory. We train a second part whose only job is to watch what has happened so far and guess what the next picture will be. Not what the game is. Not the rules. Just: given everything up to now, what comes next.

props.headline: Watch what happened. Guess what follows.
props.kicker: and it keeps a running sense of what is going on

beats.narration_text: And once it can guess the next picture, something strange becomes possible. Feed its own guess back in as if it were real, and it can keep going, and going, playing a whole game that is not happening anywhere.

So that is where we train the player. Inside the dream. It tries, it fails, it adjusts, hundreds of times over — and the real game is switched off the entire time. Then, only at the very end, we let it out to play for real.

props.headline: The real game stays switched off.
props.kicker: every bit of practice happens inside the model

beats.narration_text: And here is the finding the whole notebook is built around. We train the player twice, identically. The first one only gets to see the squeezed picture: it catches 39 percent. The second one sees the picture and also gets the memory's running sense of what has been happening: 78 percent. Same dream, same practice, same everything else.

rows.label: a cheat that sees the real ball

beats.narration_text: Look at that bottom bar again, because it is the good bit. The chaser is allowed to cheat — it sees the true ball position, perfectly, every turn. It manages 61 percent. The dreamer, working only from a blurry squeezed picture and its own memory, gets 78. Remembering beat seeing.

props.headline: A good memory beat perfect eyesight.
props.kicker: because speed lives in the past, not the present

beats.narration_text: There is a second way to use a dream, and it is the one you already use yourself. Instead of training a player at all, just imagine several things you could do, see how each one turns out, and pick the best.

And then you can go round in a circle. The trained player goes and plays for real, which produces much better experience — 63.8 of those games end in a catch instead of 28 percent. Feed that back in, the dream gets more accurate, and the player trained in the better dream reaches 84 percent.

So here is everybody, lined up by how many balls they actually caught in the real game. The random flailer at the bottom. The cheat that can see the true ball. The dreamer with no memory, barely better than flailing. And then the ones with memory, up near the top, next to something that knows the answer outright.

rows.name: greedy chaser (sees the true ball, no memory)
MPC planning in the model (64 plans)

beats.narration_text: And here is the thing worth carrying away. A single snapshot tells you what is there. It cannot tell you what is happening. For that you need to remember what came a moment ago — and that is as true for you crossing a road as it is for a machine catching a ball.

props.headline: A snapshot is not a situation.
props.kicker: what is happening only exists across time

beats.narration_text: So here is the whole thing. A tiny game. A squeezer that throws away almost everything and keeps what matters. A memory that guesses what happens next. A dream built out of those guesses. And a player that got good inside the dream, came out, and beat something that was allowed to cheat.

artifactLines: Squeeze: every 256-square picture becomes 8 numbers, 32x smaller, and 99.3% rebuild with every square correct.
Check: the ball's position is still in there — hard to read in a straight line, perfectly readable when compared against similar frames.
Remember: a second part learns only to guess the next picture, and keeps a running sense of what has been going on.
Dream: feed its own guesses back in, and it plays whole games that are not happening anywhere.
Train inside the dream: picture only, 39%. Picture plus memory, 78% — beating the 61% cheat that sees the real ball.
Go round again: better play makes better experience makes a better dream — 84%, against a perfect score of 100%.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Next time you catch something, notice what your eyes actually gave you: a stack of snapshots, and no arrows at all. The sense that the thing is moving towards you is not something you saw. Your brain built it, out of remembering. Same trick, different machine.

props.command: Explain what information a single still frame can and cannot contain about a moving object, and what a brain or a model has to add to recover motion.
output: a frame holds positions, never velocities

beats.narration_text: Practising in its sleep. If you like the ideas that turn out to be about you too, subscribe. Humanitarians AI.
